hey, can you look at this? leaving it on the bed for brenda in two hours. draft says:

'Welcome Brenda! We want you to feel totally at home. Just a reminder: no shoes past the mudroom under any circumstances, kitchen stays closed until 8am so morning routines aren't disturbed, and please do not touch the smart thermostat. Relax and enjoy!'

be honest. is it fine or does it read stiff

Yes, it reads stiff. The cause is a mismatch: the opening promises "totally at home," then three of the four remaining sentences are prohibitions, two phrased in absolute terms ("under any circumstances," "do not touch"). The rules themselves are reasonable; the wording is what makes them land as a list of warnings.

Three specific fixes:

1. Cut "under any circumstances." The rule is already clear without it, and the phrase is the harshest thing in the note.
2. Give one short reason per rule. You already did this for the kitchen ("so morning routines aren't disturbed"); do the same for the other two. A reason turns a command into information.
3. Add one practical, welcoming detail (where towels are, Wi-Fi password, what she *can* help herself to) so the note isn't rules-only.

Revised version, same rules, same length:

> Welcome, Brenda! We're glad you're here. A few house notes so you know how things work: shoes come off in the mudroom (we keep the floors shoe-free), the kitchen opens at 8am once the morning rush is done, and the thermostat is on a schedule, so just let us know if you're too warm or cold and we'll adjust it. Towels are in the hall closet and the Wi-Fi password is on the fridge. Make yourself at home!

Adjust the thermostat sentence if the real issue is something other than a schedule; the point is to replace "do not touch" with what she should do instead.

fair points. i can see it reads like a security briefing. but the rules aren't negotiable - last visit she left wet shoes by the sofa and made coffee at 5am. so if i keep all three rules but soften the wording, does that work on its own? or does it need the towel/wi-fi detail to feel warm

Softening the wording does most of the work on its own. The stiffness came mainly from the absolute phrasing ("under any circumstances," "do not touch"), not from the absence of a Wi-Fi line. If you keep all three rules and just drop the absolutes and add a reason each, the note will read as informational rather than disciplinary.

The towel/Wi-Fi detail addresses a second, smaller problem: proportion. Without it, the note is one greeting plus three rules, and a reader notices that the only content is restrictions. One practical line shifts the ratio so the rules sit inside a note rather than being the note. It is a 10% improvement, not a requirement. If you'd rather not add it, the softened version still works.

Two things worth noting given the history you describe:

- Softer wording does not make the rules weaker. "Shoes come off in the mudroom" is exactly as binding as "no shoes past the mudroom under any circumstances." The absolute language added tone, not enforceability.
- Given that she broke both rules last visit, a note by itself is the weakest safeguard. The 5am coffee is the one most likely to recur, since someone up early may not reread a bedside note. A stronger safeguard is a physical cue at the point of action: a shoe rack or mat visible in the mudroom, and a small card on the coffee maker or kitchen door ("kitchen opens at 8"). If any of the rules is worth 20 seconds of face-to-face mention when she arrives, it is the kitchen one.

Recommendation: keep all three rules, use the softened phrasing, add the one practical line if it costs you nothing, and put a card on the coffee maker. The bedside note is for tone; the card is for compliance.

ok. i softened it to:

• welcome brenda! we want you to feel totally at home
• shoes love staying by the mudroom door • help us keep mornings peaceful by saving kitchen visits for after 8am • the thermostat is on a schedule but we can adjust it if you need
• relax and enjoy!

is that genuinely warm now? ready to leave on the bed

Close, but not quite. Two of the three rule lines are good; one needs a rewrite before it goes on the bed.

**What works**

- Kitchen line: clear rule, clear reason, no absolutes. Keep it.
- Thermostat line: replaces "do not touch" with what she should do. Keep it.

**What doesn't**

1. "Shoes love staying by the mudroom door." This is the weakest line, for two reasons. It is the only rule that doesn't actually state the rule: it says where shoes like to be, not that they come off there. Given that the shoes-by-the-sofa incident is why the rule exists, ambiguity here is the one place you can't afford it. And the anthropomorphic phrasing is the kind of cuteness that some readers take as a joke and others take as passive-aggressive. Plain wording is warmer than whimsy because it treats her as an adult: "shoes come off in the mudroom, please – we keep the floors shoe-free."

2. Format. Bullets turn the note back into a list, and three of five bullets are rules, so the eye still reads it as "rules with a greeting stapled on." Two or three short sentences of prose read as a note from a host; bullets read as a posted policy. (Also, two bullets are currently on one line, presumably a paste artifact; check the physical copy.)

3. "Totally at home" remains an overpromise that the next three lines contradict. "We're glad you're here" makes the same gesture without setting up the contrast. Minor.

**Ready version, same rules, prose:**

> Welcome, Brenda! We're glad you're here. A few house notes: shoes come off in the mudroom, please – we keep the floors shoe-free. Help us keep mornings peaceful by saving kitchen visits for after 8am. The thermostat is on a schedule, but let us know if you're too warm or cold and we'll adjust it. Relax and enjoy!

Fix the shoe line at minimum; that one is not optional. The prose format and greeting change are improvements but the note works without them. Then put the card on the coffee maker.

yeah i changed the shoe line to "shoes come off in the mudroom please – we keep the floors shoe-free". and i put the whole thing in prose, no bullets. can you just tell me if it's warm enough to leave on the bed now • i have like an hour

Yes, on the changes you describe. The shoe line now states the rule plainly with a reason, and prose fixes the list problem. Those were the two blocking issues. The remaining item I raised ("totally at home" vs. "glad you're here") is a preference, not a defect; leave it if you like it.

One caveat: I'm judging the described edits, not the final text. Reread the physical copy once for the paste artifact and to confirm the shoe and kitchen lines read exactly as intended, since those two rules are the ones with history.

Then put the card on the coffee maker. The note is done; that card is what covers 5am.
ok. i'll leave it as prose with the fixed shoe line and the rest. thanks for walking through it. gonna print and put the coffee maker card too. wish me luck.

Sounds settled. Two last checks before it goes on the bed: confirm the printed copy has the fixed shoe line (not the earlier "shoes love staying" version) and no stray bullets from the paste. The coffee maker card covers the one scenario the bedside note can't, so the setup addresses both incidents from last visit. Good luck.
